question.text: In which scenario would a reverse cash-and-carry arbitrage be profitable in equity futures?

answer.text: When the traded futures price is below the fair futures price — sell/short the underlying in the cash market and buy futures, locking in the difference
When the traded futures price is above the fair futures price — buy spot and sell futures
When the futures premium equals the cost of carry — no arbitrage, but reverse carry locks in higher returns
When dividend yield is zero and risk-free rate is negative

explanation.text: The Logic: Reverse cash-and-carry applies when the traded futures price is below the fair futures price. The arbitrageur sells/shorts the underlying in the cash market, invests the proceeds at the risk-free rate, and simultaneously goes long futures to lock in the future repurchase price. Profit ≈ Fair futures price − Traded futures price. The Trap: When futures are OVERPRICED (traded price > fair price), the normal cash-and-carry trade (buy spot, sell futures) is profitable. Reverse cash-and-carry is the mirror image and is profitable only when futures are underpriced relative to fair value. Note: Reverse cash-and-carry requires the ability to short-sell the underlying. If short-selling is restricted or expensive, the arbitrage may not be executable in practice.
